items.title: GDPx agent benchmark: cost per point for 12 models, and the safety-filter caveat
items.story_key: story|title:gdpx agent benchmark cost per point for 12 models and the safety filter caveat
items.content_excerpt: SemiAnalysis built GDPx, 206 long agent tasks across 11 expert fields, and the best model scored 12 percent. We worked out what each model pays per point, pulled the caveats SemiAnalysis states into the open, and walked through the one task that shows how strict the grading is. SemiAnalysis published GDPx on November 2, 2026 as a benchmark for general agent work in high-value fields: chip design, cybersecurity, biology, finance, legal, quant trading, recursive self-improvement, hardware design, materials science, alignment and software engineering. The leaderboard lists 206 tasks from 14 data partners. Tasks run up to 8 hours by default. One finance task drops the agent into a deal room of about 2,000 files. Models run in their own harness where one exists, such as Claude Code or Codex, and in OpenCode otherwise. The headline score averages the 11 fields equally, and each partner equally within a field, using each task's own grading over 3 attempts. SemiAnalysis lists an average cost per task next to each score. Dividing one by the other gives what each point of GDPx costs. These are our numbers, computed from the leaderboard; SemiAnalysis does not publish this column. Muse Wonder Full scores 9.0 percent but has no public price, so it has no cost per point. Two readings follow. If you need the single best result, Opus 5.5 leads. If you run many attempts and keep the best, Gemini 4 Carbon gets 91 percent of Opus's score for about a third of the cost per task, and GPT 6.1 Sol gets 70 percent of it for under a fifth. On binary grading, every model scored 0 percent in finance. One finance task, Bellwood-QoE, went unsolved across 25 attempts, and the best run passed 8 of 11 checks. In legal, 20 rollouts produced no usable contract redline, though partial scores averaged 44 percent for Opus 5.5 and 25 percent for GPT-6 Astra. In hardware design, none of 12 rollouts reached a verified full pass. In the recursive self-improvement task, none of 20 rollouts reliably found the cause of a broken RL harness. The public quant task aapl-target-winsorization asks the agent to beat a reference trading strategy on hidden days. A strategy scores 1 only if a one-sided paired t-test on daily profit gives p below 0.01, and 0 if p is above 0.5. The reference is scaled up when the agent takes more risk. 10 of 12 runs made more than the reference's $1,399 out of sample, yet only 2 reached a score of 0.5. One Opus 5.5 run made $2,540 at 1.3 times the risk and scored 0.23. A Grok 4.

items.title: The Iron(wood) Throne: Google's TPU Stakes Its Claim on Inference
items.summary: Viable Alternative of CUDA Moat, NVIDIA scared and working nights & weekends, Jensen’s Counter Submission, Kimi K3, Muse Spark Open, Qwen, GLM5.3, TorchTPU, vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, Ray
items.story_key: story|title:the iron wood throne google s tpu stakes its claim on inference
items.content_excerpt: In November 2025, we published a newsletter saying that Google is selling TPUs to external customers. Since then, we have been proven right over and over again with Oracle, OpenAI , Anthropic, and Meta all becoming customers of TPUs just as our Accelerator Model reported. Hardware demand is only half the story, as NVIDIA’s moat has historically been its software and large developer ecosystem. This is where TPU is also making headway, partnering with upstream maintainers across the entire ecosystem, including the Meta PyTorch team, vLLM (Inferact, RedHat), SGLang (RadixArk), llm-d, Ray, etc. This is not a surprise to folks that have read our September 2026 article laying out Google TPU’s externalization strategy . Back in our September article, we published the first third-party TPUv7 results on InferenceX on single-turn workloads, showing that in an apples-to-apples FP8 comparison on Qwen 3.5 397B, TPUv7 Ironwood) delivered up to 50% better performance per dollar than B200 and B300. We also reported that many Google TPU customers were asking for AgentX results, since long-context, multi-turn agentic serving is where inference spend is heading. Previously, Jensen went on the Dwarkesh Podcast and commented on the fact that no other chips were taking advantage of their opportunity to show performance on InferenceX. Six months later, and indeed Google is taking full advantage of this opportunity. Today we are releasing the first official long-context, multi-turn, realistic agentic inference benchmark results on TPUv7 across four models, showing that TPUv7 is either competitive on perf per dollar for external customers or delivers the best state-of-the-art result: Muse Spark Open SGLang AgentX (NVFP4 weights): Competitive TPU performance per dollar result even though the architecture was co-designed for GPUs. Submitted by OSS ecosystem developer, RadixArk (Makers of SGLang). GLM-5.2 vLLM AgentX (FP8): TPUv7 is the cheapest FP8 option, delivering 1.2x to 2.7x the tokens per dollar of B200, B300, and MI355X from 60 to 300 tok/s/user. NVIDIA NVFP4 still beats TPUv7 FP8, but with accuracy / quality loss. Qwen3.5 vLLM AgentX (FP8): With llm-d disaggregated serving, TPUv7 beats GB300 FP8 at every interactivity level and restores parity even against GB300 FP4 at higher quality / accuracy. Kimi K3 vLLM AgentX (MXFP4 weights): Competitive with GB300 NVL72 at launch; With TPUv7 delivering 1.15x to 2.5x the tokens per dollar of GB200, B200, B300, and MI355X. Submitted by

items.title: Distributed Inference Benchmarks: [K]Inference vs. Plain Kubernetes
items.story_key: story|title:distributed inference benchmarks k inference vs plain kubernetes
items.content_excerpt: Kinference (“kay-inference") is an inference control plane for Kubernetes and vLLM . Kinference sits in front of a heterogeneous set of GPUs and models, each with different capabilities and levels of performance; takes inference requests from a set of heterogeneous clients, each with different requirements and competing demands; and figures out how to satisfy the clients without overloading the cluster. And it gives you declarative policies to determine exactly how that happens. Part of how Kinference delivers on its promise is by load balancing inference requests based on predicted TTFT . In other words, given an inference request (a “prompt”), Kinference predicts the time-to-first-token (TTFT) for that request against each candidate endpoint, then sends it to the worker (e.g. vLLM pod) with the lowest predicted latency. TTFT is a good metric for this because it’s independent of the output size, and because load balancing here can make a tremendous difference–sometimes multiple orders of magnitude. To make these TTFT predictions, Kinference makes use of a variety of data about the underlying vLLM pods, including contents of their KV cache . The KV cache is where inference workers store intermediate results of the prefill phase of inference computation. These results may be reused on future requests–but only if they share a prefix. Since many inference requests share a substantial prefix (for example, successive turns in the same conversation), sending a request to a worker with a high KV cache overlap can save a tremendous amount of time. In this benchmark, we attempt to quantify exactly how much Kinference’s intelligent load balancing helps, by comparing inference requests to a multi-pod vLLM deployment with Kinference against the same requests without Kinference. Measuring unloaded latency demonstrates the value of KV-cache-aware load balancing in isolation, i.e. independent of queueing and other factors. Measuring capacity within an SLO, by contrast, demonstrates real-world performance: how does KV-cache-aware balancing improve a system’s overall ability to serve inference traffic? To test our metrics, we created an AWS cluster where we deployed two identical pools of vLLM 0.31.0, running the Qwen-3.8-27B-FP8 open weight model. Each pool comprised 3 vLLM pods, each running on its own L40S GPU. The two arms of our test were two OpenAI chat-completion HTTP endpoints: one from Kinference, pointing to the first vLLM pool, and one from the Kubernetes Servic

items.title: Show HN: Umbel – Remote-control agent CLIs over tmux
items.summary: Been using this in all my sessions the last months. Opus 5.5 (over MCP) spawns Deepseek flash agents - and codex for audits etc. Very curious to hear what the HN crowd thinks/makes of it.
items.story_key: story|title:umbel remote control agent clis over tmux
items.content_excerpt: Remote-control interactive agent CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini) over tmux. One binary, three faces, one provider abstraction. Spawn other-provider agent workers from inside your agent session. Drive claude , codex , gemini , or opencode interactively in tmux from a CLI, MCP server, or YAML workflow. One binary, one provider abstraction — subscription-billed for claude/codex/gemini, bring-any-model for opencode. Your claude session can't spawn a codex session directly. With umbel mcp configured, it can: Your Claude Code agent now has umbel_spawn , umbel_send , umbel_wait , umbel_read , umbel_kill , and umbel_help in its toolbelt. Tell it: Spawn a Codex reviewer in ./worktrees/a and a Gemini tester in ./worktrees/b . Have them work in parallel, then synthesize their findings. It'll stand up both workers, dispatch the prompts, wait for completion, and read their outputs. Three subscriptions, three roles, one orchestration. The host's context stays clean — it spends tokens on planning and synthesis, not on doing the work itself. The server ships a server-level instructions block plus an on-demand umbel_help tool (topics: lifecycle , workflow , providers ) so your agent learns when to reach for umbel and how to use it without being drowned in upfront context. The same verbs from your shell — useful in scripts, cron, or when driving umbel without an MCP host: A single supervisor can drive workers across providers concurrently. The provider is recorded in meta.json per session so send / wait / read / kill auto-route — no --provider needed after spawn. Full verb list: spawn , send , wait , status , ls , kill , attach , read , capture , logs , run , mcp . --provider defaults to claude (so umbel -p mirrors claude -p ). Cold-start ~3–5s on first call; use --name / --resume to keep a session warm: Providers without their binary installed simply can't be selected. umbel spawn --provider gemini fails loudly when tmux can't exec gemini . No daemon. tmux is the daemon; ~/.umbel/ is the state store. Every umbel invocation is short-lived. Completion detection uses each provider's native lifecycle event (Claude Stop , Codex Stop , Gemini AfterAgent , OpenCode session.status idle) — not terminal scraping. Agent output is read from each provider's transcript (JSONL for claude/codex/gemini; opencode export JSON for opencode), never from capture-pane . Providers are pluggable via a small interface ( src/core/providers/types.ts ) — adding a new CLI is a ~150 LOC implementation

items.title: Agents Are Going Async
items.summary: Async subagents let an agent stay responsive while background workers run long tasks. How the orchestrator, notifications and approvals work in Deep Agents.
items.story_key: story|title:agents are going async
items.content_excerpt: Imagine a chief of staff who disappears every time you hand them a big project and only comes back once it's done. You'd probably fire them immediately. A good chief of staff keeps projects moving in the background while staying reachable and keeping you updated along the way. As we ask agents to work toward bigger goals, they need the same two properties. An agent has to be responsive, acting on a new instruction right away with the context of everything before it, and productive, making progress on many large tasks at once. The architecture we've used to build agents for a while can't meet both requirements. In a standard ReAct loop, each long tool call blocks the loop and every other task queues behind it. Instead, we're seeing the ecosystem converge on a split between one agent that stays with the user and background workers that do the long work. Claude Code runs subagents in the background by default, OpenAI's dots hand work to background workers to make progress on several things at once, and DeepSeek Harness built its super agent around a router that talks to people and background workers that run tasks in parallel. We’re bringing this pattern to Deep Agents with async subagents . An orchestrator stays available to the user and keeps the conversation's context organized, while async subagents run as background workers and report back when they finish. The amount of work the agent can take on then grows with the number of background workers instead of the length of one loop. An agent runs in a loop. The model calls a tool, waits for the result, and decides what to do next. Historically, tools and subagents blocked that loop until they returned, like code that awaits each slow call in turn. An async subagent works like a task started with asyncio.create_task or a Promise you don't await yet. The call returns right away, the work runs independently in the background, and the result comes back later. Steering a running subagent is separate from reaching the orchestrator. When the orchestrator sends a follow-up with update_async_task , the update_strategy field on that subagent's definition decides what happens: Every unfinished task is listed in the orchestrator's system prompt, so it always knows what's in flight. It can poll with check_async_task or tasks can report back on their own : A subagent that needs approval shows up as waiting , and the user answers on the subagent's own thread without interrupting the orchestrator. items.title: New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation
items.story_key: story|title:new nvidia cosmos 3 open models for interactive world simulation
items.content_excerpt: NVIDIA Cosmos world model development platform adds four new open-weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family for generating interactive world simulation and multi-sensor multi-view driving scenes: All four models are post-trained examples of Cosmos 3 Nano and have 16B trainable parameters. The models use OpenMDW1.1, permitting commercial and non-commercial use under its terms. 🦾 Robotics needs environments that can answer this across changing scenes and viewpoints. These checkpoints offer complementary ways to build them: Sim-Bimanual predicts visual consequences from actions, while Sim-Transfer turns a physics simulator’s controls into generated observations. 🚦 For autonomous driving, appearance and geometry must agree. Synchronized camera and LiDAR generation connects visual observations with 3D sensing. Scene and traffic-signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, then study how a driving policy responds. 🔄 Each observation can shape the next action. Streaming generation connects video prediction to ongoing interaction, giving world-model researchers a way to explore how actions and observations unfold together. 🌐 An open foundation for others to build on. NVIDIA’s vision is to help researchers and developers create richer, more responsive simulated worlds. Open weights and post-training recipes provide a shared starting point for adapting models, comparing methods, and contributing improvements. These problems remain hard: the work ahead is to measure where the models faithfully support policy learning and evaluation, understand their limits, and improve where they fall short. Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto is a bidirectional model for offline synthetic driving data generation. It generates synchronized video across up to 11 camera views, including fisheyes, and supports joint RGB–LiDAR generation. Per-camera World Scenario Map (WSM) controls specify scene structure and traffic motion, while text prompts guide appearance. Developers can vary environmental conditions to expand training and evaluation coverage, with optional initial RGB images to anchor scene appearance. Joint LiDAR generation additionally uses aligned HD-map range-map controls. Transfer-Auto also serves as the foundation for adapting Cosmos to your own sensor rig and driving domain. items.title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast, cost-effective, and reliable video generation and editing now generally available
items.summary:
Today, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is generally available on Google Cloud. Built for the everyday videos businesses make in volume — like product videos, virtual try-ons, and ads — this model is fast, cost-effective, and follows your image, video and audio references more closely than before.  

Business users can create with it in Gemini for business and Google Vids, and developers can build with it via API.

Here's what's new:

  • A lower price: $0.07 per second of 720p video, 30% less than Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash, with similar savings at other resolutions.
  • Longer clips: Generate and edit videos of up to 15 seconds, up from 10s.
  • More consistent results: stronger adherence to image and video references keeps products, characters, and brand details consistent from shot to shot.
  • Faster drafts, in higher resolution: create drafts at 360p or 720p, then upscale the best creations to 1080p or 4K.
  • More natural speech: You can generate scenes with more fluid, natural-sounding dialogue, clearer lip-sync, and distinct multi-speaker conditioning.
  • Editing in conversation: refine the same clip, such as swapping a product, changing lighting, or changing camera angle, instead of starting over.

Note: Audio references are gated behind allowlisting.

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is ready for production

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is production-ready and backed by Google Cloud’s enterprise-grade infrastructure and security, offering Provisioned Throughput. Outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark.

Video creation inside the tools people already use

Design and creative platforms are building Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash directly into their products, so their users can create and edit videos where they already work. Here’s how customers are already using Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash:

“At Artlist, we’re focused on giving creators the control and flexibility to bring their ideas to life. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash brings exciting capabilities in reference-based generation, video extension, and creative consistency, helping our customers move from experimentation to professional content production at scale.” – Roee Peled, CPTO, Artlist.

Artlist uses Gemini 1.2 Omni Flash to bring creative ideas to life

“Creative teams need models that they can rely on consistently. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash edits exactly what you ask for, a colorway or a background, and leaves the product untouched, even from detailed images and finished video. Its video-to-video takes footage into entirely new styles.” – Andrew Taco Zhang, Product Marketing Manager, FLORA.

FLORA uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to create new styles

“We ran Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash through our evals at invideo. Honestly, it's really good. It sticks to the prompt, and the physics and sound feel real. If you need fast video at scale, it's one of the best we've tested. And 15 seconds means a full scene in one go.” – Shivam Rastogi, VP of Engineering, invideo.

invideo uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to create full scenes in one prompt

“We’re really impressed by how fast and accurate this new model is. The outputs retain an amazing level of detail, and the model does a great job of making only the changes we ask for while keeping everything else consistent. We’re excited to use it for character and scene replacements, as well as other creative workflows.” – Numan Khan, Creative Specialist, Krea.

Krea uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash for their creative workflows, from character to scene replacements

"Gemini Omni 1.2 fits the way our teams work. Draft mode lets us iterate concepts in minutes, then render in 4K for TV-ready AI dramas. Text stays crisp across frames, characters look and sound real, and the speed keeps production moving. Now that it is generally available, we can bring this quality to over 100M Picsart creators." – Narek Hayrapetyan, Head of Product and Partnerships, Picsart.

Picsart uses Gemini 1.2 Flash to iterate concepts in minutes

Runway empowers creatives with advanced AI video tools to produce high-quality content. For organizations, Runway’s enterprise solutions deliver robust collaborative tools to scale professional production. Here is what they created with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash.

Runway uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to produce and scale high-quality content

Product and listing videos at catalog scale

Retailers and marketplaces use Gemini Omni to turn the photos they already have into short product spins, lifestyle clips, try-on videos, and video ads.

“Photoroom turns product photos into video ads that sell in minutes. We chose Gemini Omni Flash to power our Video Ad Maker and Product Animator because it balances quality, speed and cost. Version 1.2 brings 15-second videos, a top user request. With general availability and SLAs, we can rely on it in production for our sellers and enterprise customers.” - Matt Rouif, CEO and Co-founder, Photoroom.

Photoroom uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to power their Video Ad Maker and Product Animator

“QuickFrame AI helps marketers and business owners create, edit, and launch professional-quality ads for CTV and social in minutes. With Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash now supporting 15-second video generations at 1080p, users can create a complete CTV ad in a single generation, making TV ad creation simpler for businesses of all sizes.” - Richard Girges, Chief Technology Officer, QuickFrame AI.

QuickFrame AI uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to create complete CTV ads in a single generation

Create in Gemini for business, Google Vids and build with the API

Coming soon to Gemini, business users will be able to create a short video from a prompt or a product photo, right in the chat. In Google Vids, teams can combine generated clips with avatars, music and voiceover to create product explainers, teasers, social posts and sales pitches. Businesses can also embed the capabilities of Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash into their applications and agents via the API.

Get started with Gemini Omni

We'll keep improving Gemini Omni based on your feedback, so tell us what you build.

  • For business users: Try it in Google Vids; coming soon to Gemini for business

  • For developers: Try it in the Google Cloud console, build with the API, and see the pricing

items.title: GeoFaham: Domain-Specialized Multi-Agent Geospatial Analytics for Disaster Response
items.summary: Real-world geospatial decision support requires more than single-step retrieval or code generation. Disaster-response questions often involve multi-source workflows that combine spatial databases, map-derived features, satellite imagery, raster products, and reusable geospatial artifacts, where correctness depends on preserving spatial scope, temporal context, and intermediate execution state. While large language models and coding agents offer a promising interface for such workflows, they struggle with geospatial-specific failure modes, including handling large artifacts, selecting the wrong evidence source, losing spatial or temporal metadata, and applying invalid geometric operations. We introduce GeoFaham, a domain-specialized multi-agent system for geospatial disaster analytics. GeoFaham decomposes workflows into specialist agents for vector operations, map feature retrieval, imagery discovery, and raster analysis, coordinated by an Orchestrator with a dual-ledger control loop for dependency-aware planning, progress tracking, validation, and replanning. To support artifact-centric collaboration, GeoFaham uses a Response Store that persists full geospatial outputs and typed metadata outside the LLM context window while agents exchange compact identifiers and summaries. We also introduce GeoFaham-Bench, a 40-task benchmark grounded in 17 real-world disaster records, designed to evaluate multi-step geospatial reasoning, cross-source integration, raster-vector computation, artifact generation, and recovery under non-rigid ground truth. We evaluate GeoFaham on GeoFaham-Bench against strong general-purpose coding-agent baselines, including Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode. GeoFaham achieves the best overall performance, scoring 0.940 versus the next-best 0.879, while using 7.5 times fewer tokens. Our code and benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/GeoFaham.

items.title: TestBED: An Open-Source Toolkit for Bayesian Experimental Design
items.summary: Bayesian experimental design (BED) is a principled framework for intelligent data acquisition with applications across a wide range of scientific and industrial domains. However, the development and adoption of BED remains hindered by a lack of standardised software and benchmarks. Existing methods are typically implemented in bespoke codebases and evaluated on a small subset of tasks, making methods difficult to apply, compare, or extend. To address this, we present TestBED, a general-purpose, open-source toolkit for Bayesian experimental design. TestBED decomposes the BED process into modular, reusable components spanning tasks, objectives, training mechanisms, policy architectures, and evaluation procedures, together with scalable implementations of core primitives such as expected information gain estimators. We provide a wide range of these components, which can be freely composed, allowing existing methods to be reproduced within a common framework, while also enabling previously unexplored configurations and new methodologies to be easily implemented and evaluated. Using TestBED, we further conduct a large-scale benchmark of contemporary BED methods, including controlled studies of under-appreciated but surprisingly critical methodological choices, such as the importance of time embeddings in design policy architectures. By providing a modular, extensible software foundation and a reproducible benchmarking suite, we hope that TestBED will accelerate methodological research in BED and lower the barrier to its real-world application.

items.title: Energy-Guided Transport for Projection-Free Physics-Informed Flow Matching
items.summary: Deep generative models, particularly Flow Matching frameworks, have emerged as powerful tools for synthesizing complex physical systems. However, standard architectures remain purely statistically driven and agnostic to the underlying governing equations, often violating fundamental physical constraints during inference. Existing zero-shot approaches designed to enforce these constraints typically rely on rigid algebraic projections. While effective for sparse boundary conditions, applying such discrete geometric corrections to dense, full-domain PDEs may disrupt the probability path, \rev{potentially deviating from the learned manifold and introducing substantial computational overhead}. To address these challenges, we introduce Energy-Guided Transport, a novel training-free framework that formulates non-linear physical constraints as a smooth potential energy landscape. Rather than interrupting the ODE integration, our method applies a continuous dissipative force directly to the intermediate generative states, steering them toward the physical manifold. By evaluating this force implicitly via reverse-mode automatic differentiation, our framework preserves the natural dynamics of the flow while maintaining an efficient $\mathcal{O}(N)$ algorithmic complexity. We extensively evaluate our framework across various 1D and 2D physical systems, including the chaotic Navier-Stokes equations. Our method achieves stable generation without structural divergence, significantly improves the stability-accuracy trade-off compared to state-of-the-art methods, and substantially accelerates inference with respect to exact projection strategies. Code available at: https://github.com/ispamm/Projection-free-energy-guided-flow-matching.

items.title: SAUCE: Summary Analysis Using Conversation Entailment
items.summary: With the growing need for evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) and their applications to speech, challenges persist in summarizing and evaluating conversations that lack a clear end goal. We introduce SAUCE -- a reference-free, fact-based evaluation pipeline for cross-lingual conversational speech summarization. It measures the accuracy and the fact coverage of a summary through the entailment between conversation and text. We compare SAUCE against several popular summarization metrics and demonstrate the effectiveness of capturing information loss due to transcription and translation error and identifying broken summaries. Crucially, unlike black-box LLM evaluators or dense embedding metrics, SAUCE is inherently explainable: it maps summary scores to discrete, verifiable facts, allowing users to pinpoint exact hallucinations or omissions. We illustrate how this interpretability helps developers systematically profile LLM behaviors and gives end-users an actionable tool to verify summary accuracy in noisy, real-world conditions. Preliminary investigations show SAUCE strongly align with human judgment.

items.content_excerpt: How Delta Sharing became OpenSharing, an open, vendor-neutral protocol that extends zero-copy sharing beyond tables to agent skills, AI models, and unstructured data across platforms, and what the change means if you already share data today. Delta Sharing has been the way thousands of organizations exchange live data across clouds and platforms without copying it. In June 2026, Databricks and the Linux Foundation announced that Delta Sharing has evolved into OpenSharing , an open, vendor-neutral protocol for sharing not just tables, but the broader set of assets that AI teams now depend on: agent skills, AI models, and unstructured data. If you already share data with Delta Sharing, or you're evaluating how to collaborate with partners on both data and AI assets, this post walks through what OpenSharing actually is, what's changed under the hood, and where the project is headed. When Databricks introduced Delta Sharing at Data + AI Summit 2021, the core problem it addressed was simple to state and hard to solve well: organizations wanted to share live data with partners, customers, and other teams, without exporting files, standing up brittle ETL jobs, or forcing every recipient onto the same platform. Delta Sharing was contributed to the Linux Foundation as an open protocol, built on Delta Lake and Parquet, so a provider could grant access to a table and a recipient could query it directly, in real time, from tools like Apache Spark, Power BI, Tableau, pandas, and many others. That open, zero-copy model resonated. Delta Sharing grew into the most widely adopted open protocol for secure data sharing, used by organizations including Amadeus, Atlassian, LSEG, SAP, Stripe, and The Trade Desk for cross-cloud and cross-platform collaboration, according to Databricks ( Databricks press release ). By the time Databricks announced OpenSharing in June 2026, Delta Sharing had reached more than 28,000 data recipients, with roughly a third of shares flowing across platforms through open connectors rather than staying inside Databricks-to-Databricks sharing ( Databricks blog ). Sharing had already grown well beyond tables. Through Databricks-to-Databricks sharing, teams were exchanging views, volumes of unstructured files, notebooks, and registered ML models years before agents entered the picture, so structured data was never the whole story. What agents changed was the kind of asset that needed to move, and how far it needed to travel. Agent skills, the agents thems

items.title: How big is the open model economy today?
items.summary: Our first open model economy research note for paid subscribers.
items.story_key: story|title:how big is the open model economy today
items.content_excerpt: My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. This dashboard is freely available and becoming quite useful. Still, all the measurements we have on open model adoption are incredibly imprecise. We have noisy platform metrics, marketing-related metrics from startups, and imperfect public evaluations. It takes an informed eye to figure out where things are going. These research notes are my current best approximations of where we stand. As with most things on Interconnects, our goal is to build well more value than we capture, so the data on the dashboard will remain free for the foreseeable future. These notes will be more raw than many of my articles, a place for sharing what I’m mulling over but don’t have complete evidence for (yet). They will be primarily paid, enabling me to speak more freely. If you work in AI policy or policy-facing research, please reach out to us and we can likely get discounted or free access. The primary question I wanted to address today is: What is the market for open model inference? Is it growing? Is it a rounding error relative to OpenAI/Anthropic? I’ve been building the best measurements I can here, primarily using the open model inference startups Baseten, Fireworks, and Together AI as the bellwethers here (along with the open model share of OpenRouter’s token volume, which they thankfully report in their API). The hyperscalers also likely have a major footprint here, e.g. Amazon Bedrock and Azure’s model garden, but I haven’t seen them break down usage by model category. The startups’ fates are much more directly correlated with the success of open model inference as a category. For the latest data, we can start with a slide from my talk on the open model economy (recording here ). These are the public disclosures from the open model startups on their token volume, over time, log-scale. This shows near-exponential growth, before the uptick that would follow GLM 5.2’s step change in open agents . For example, Fireworks announced at their first company conference this week that they’re serving more than 40T tokens per day to customers’ customized models. This is just one slice of their inference, a vertical that they said grew over 2x from this summer, so I would expect their total number this fall to be well above 100T tokens when we get the next update. items.title: Maggie Appleton: Agentic Coding Has Outgrown the Text Box
items.summary:
Agentic coding has outgrown the text box. Maggie Appleton, staff research engineer at GitHub Next, argues that walls of CLI output and AGENTS.md files serve coding agents far better than the humans steering them. She walks through Chopin, the GitHub Next prototype where background agents turn a team's planning chat into a structured plan, and makes the case for agents that prompt you instead of waiting to be prompted.

What we cover:
– Why text-heavy agentic coding tools favor agents over humans
– Boundary objects: what AGENTS.md, skill files and MCP servers get right and wrong
– Multiplayer planning with coding agents in GitHub Next's Chopin
– Human-to-agent handoffs, formal verification and spec-driven development
– Why software quality is rising, not falling, with coding agents
– Which roles still matter: PMs, designers and engineers

items.title: vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for Kimi K3.1 Pro
items.summary: vLLM supports Kimi K3.1 Pro on day 0: sparse attention on a KDA hybrid, a packed KV cache with FP8 or NVFP4 latents and MXFP4 index keys, token-sharded prefill, decode context parallelism, and fused low-latency decode.
items.story_key: model:vllm|ver:3.1|variant:pro|title:vllm delivers day 0 support for kimi k3 1 pro
items.content_excerpt: Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI's most capable open-weight model: a 2.8T-parameter (104B active) multimodal MoE with a 1M-token context that matches the strongest closed-source models on coding, agentic and knowledge benchmarks. The main change is attention: K3.1 Pro adds Sparse Attention (DSA) to all 24 full-attention layers for efficiency. vLLM supports it on day 0 on NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, Google TPUs and Alibaba T-Head Zhenwu PPUs. Each sparse attention layer has a small indexer next to its MLA attention. The indexer keeps one FP8 key per token (132 bytes with its scale) and scores every earlier token for each query with 32 lightweight heads. Then it keeps the top 2,048 tokens. MLA attention then runs exactly, but only over those 2,048 tokens. DSA was introduced in DeepSeek-V3.2; our DeepSeek-V3.2 post covers the indexer in more detail. The payoff is largest in long-context decode, which is bound by memory bandwidth. Dense MLA reads 576 bytes of FP8 latent per context token per layer. DSA still scans the whole context, but only the 132-byte index keys. It then reads the full latent for just 2,048 tokens. At long context, that is about 23% of the bytes dense MLA reads per layer. Figure 1: Sparse attention (DSA) in Kimi K3.1 Pro. The indexer scores every past token, keeps the top 2,048, and every query head attends exactly over only those tokens' latents. Step through it. The index keys are a second per-token cache next to the MLA latent. Under tensor parallelism (TP) both are replicated on every GPU; KDA state is per request, as in K3. The latent and the index keys can be quantized independently. An NVFP4 latent alone already brings K3.1 Pro below K3 with FP8. Opt-in MXFP4 index keys fit 11% more tokens on top and make the indexer 10–20% faster at long context. With both, eight GB300 GPUs hold 1.7× as many tokens as with FP8, and DCP8 multiplies that by seven: about 36 full 1M-token contexts at once, against 3 for TP8 with FP8. Figure 2: Measured KV cache capacity on 8× GB300. Change the latent and index-key formats, the parallelism, or the context length to see how many full contexts fit. Each DSA layer stores two per-token caches of different widths: the MLA latent (576 bytes in FP8, 352 in NVFP4) and the index keys (132 bytes in FP8, 68 in MXFP4). Neither width is a multiple of the other. The 69 KDA layers each add a recurrent state per request that is much larger than one layer's page of tokens. items.title: claude-code v2.1.314
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added permissions.blockWritesOutsideWorkingDirectories: Write, Edit and NotebookEdit refuse paths outside the working directories in every permission mode
  • Added an optional groups list to Claude apps gateway upstreams: only developers in the listed IdP groups are sent to that upstream, on failover too
  • Added guardrail_trace to Claude apps gateway Bedrock upstreams, to log which Amazon Bedrock guardrail filter fired on a request, without the matched text
  • Added idle compaction to VS Code and Claude Desktop's Code tab: a 200K+ token conversation left idle is summarized, and the summary is used on your next message if the prompt cache has expired
  • Fixed sessions failing turn after turn with "Invalid effort level" when an organization's admin caps a model's effort: Claude Code now lowers the effort, retries, and says which level it uses
  • Fixed claude -p exiting with code 0 and no output when startup failed; it now prints the error and exits 1
  • Fixed Bedrock sessions with many images failing every turn and /compact with "400 Input is too long." instead of removing older images and compacting
  • Fixed Microsoft Foundry sessions failing when the resource has no deployment for the default Sonnet, Opus or Haiku model: Claude Code now falls back to an older model of that family
  • Fixed repeated refused requests behind a gateway that doesn't accept tool search's tool_reference blocks: the request is sent again once without tool search, and the session remembers
  • Fixed TLS connections failing with UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT when the system certificate store holds a renewed root certificate that is cross-signed with its predecessor
  • Fixed MCP servers that also work without sign-in showing "needs authentication" after their stored sign-in stopped working; they are now used signed out
  • Fixed claude mcp logout reporting success when the MCP sign-in was not removed, for example while the macOS keychain is locked over SSH
  • Fixed extra sign-in renewals when several sessions share an Anthropic profile login and the credentials lock is busy
  • Fixed claude ultrareview and claude remote-control asking the workspace trust question in a CI job that has a terminal; with CI set they now refuse an untrusted folder at once
  • Fixed an administrator's TLS trust settings in managed settings not being applied in Claude Desktop sessions
  • Fixed model switching being refused on machines with managed plugin settings when one of your own --plugin-dir or --plugin-url plugins had a broken manifest or failed to download
  • Fixed the Bedrock and Vertex model upgrade offer coming back at every start when managed settings pin the model
  • Fixed forceRemoteSettingsRefresh set only in remote managed settings no longer applying once the stored copy had expired, which let sessions start without policy when the server could not be reached
  • Fixed "Continue automatically at usage limit" continuing more than three times without a prompt from you when a task restarted itself between waits (a /goal check-in, a background or scheduled task)
  • Fixed background and cloud sessions started with Ultracode turning it back on at their next start after it had been switched off
  • Fixed the last broken reply and its retry prompts staying in the conversation after Claude gave up on a tool call that could not be parsed
  • Fixed a PreCompact hook with very large output making compaction fail or repeat; each hook's output is now cut at 10,000 characters
  • Fixed background diff refreshes briefly taking the repository's index lock, which could make a git command run at the same moment fail with "Unable to create '.git/index.lock': File exists"
  • Fixed markdown tables jumping between grid and stacked layouts on half-typed rows while streaming, and long tables falling back to raw pipes
  • Fixed the /resume picker showing the text of CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md as a session's title when the session only ran slash commands
  • Fixed /btw answering from the main conversation when asked from a subagent's open transcript
  • Fixed pasting an image over SSH to a Linux machine doing nothing silently; the prompt now says to copy the file over and paste its path
  • Fixed claude remote-control sessions that failed to start when the session service was slow for a moment: the worker's registration is now retried with growing waits
  • Fixed model switches over Remote Control that take over 8 seconds getting a "still pending" error instead of the final result
  • Fixed the sandbox.excludedCommands setting description saying listed commands always run outside the sandbox; it now says every command in a call must match an entry
  • Fixed shell and MCP calls that auto mode, a deny rule or a PreToolUse hook blocked, or that otherwise did not run, reading as if they ran in a collapsed tool group
  • Fixed sandbox protections not applying to a worktree entered by claude -p --resume or --continue
  • Fixed hooks matching Bash not running on shell commands started by the Monitor tool; such hooks can block or ask, but not approve or rewrite those commands
  • Fixed a settings file excluded with --setting-sources still supplying some settings, such as auto mode rules and saved permission consents
  • Fixed auto mode reporting a call as blocked, and listing it in /permissions, when its safety check gave no verdict
  • Fixed a Claude apps gateway Vertex upstream hanging for minutes when a Google token endpoint accepts the connection and never answers
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway's start-up warning for a deprecated Claude Desktop key that it still serves as written saying "stops being accepted" after the key's end date
  • Fixed /upgrade opening the browser and starting a new login for plans billed through the App Store or Google Play; it now says where to change the plan
  • Fixed --resume, and rewinding past a switch to another model after a refusal, moving a session on a model name Claude Code doesn't recognize to a different model
  • Fixed requests failing when a gateway or cloud provider refuses one of Claude Code's beta headers by name: the request is sent again without it
  • Fixed model IDs spelled with a dot behind an LLM gateway, such as claude-opus-4.8, being treated as an older model with the wrong context window, output limit, effort, thinking mode and cost
  • Fixed Remote Control clients showing a stray "Compacted (ctrl+o to see full summary)" row after /compact
  • Fixed the cloud sessions tip and the Remote Control idle notice showing when an organization's policy turns those features off
  • Fixed a resumed claude.ai cloud session making a model call nobody asked for when the previous worker stopped just after receiving a new chat's files
  • Fixed WebFetch in Cowork cloud sessions silently dropping a PDF's text past 100,000 characters; it now says how much was unread and where to read on
  • Fixed Claude being told only that a command was declined after you stopped it with Esc or Stop in a cloud session or the IDE; it now also hears that the command may have run
  • Fixed blank lines at the top of a code block disappearing when the code block opens a quote
  • Fixed a blank line appearing above some ⎿ rows in the transcript view (Ctrl+O)
  • Fixed vim mode dw, dW, yw and yW carrying on past the end of the line, and made w and W stop on empty lines
  • Fixed x and Enter in the agent panel sometimes acting on the wrong agent when another agent started or finished
  • Fixed pasted text and dragged-in files being lost in Claude's question dialog unless the "Other" row had focus
  • Fixed pasted text being lost when a row in the prompt footer was selected
  • Fixed vim mode p over a character selection ignoring whether the yanked text was whole lines
  • Fixed vim mode aw and iw taking the line break at the end of a line
  • Fixed ↓ selecting footer items hidden by the ? help menu, the command list or a paste hint
  • Fixed Esc on a command's panel, such as /btw, also interrupting the subagent whose transcript is open
  • Fixed the welcome header in fullscreen mode showing the session's model while viewing a subagent or teammate that runs on a different model
  • Fixed the fullscreen transcript being left mid-conversation after "Restore conversation" in the rewind menu while scrolled up
  • Fixed a rare case where a deleted session could reappear in the resume list as an almost empty entry
  • Fixed prompts containing tags such as <bash-stdout> or <local-command-stdout> not being acknowledged to a local stream-json host
  • Fixed sessions staying untitled when the first prompt failed (for example on a usage limit) and the conversation continued afterward
  • Fixed the skill file watcher checking every removed skill kept in ~/.claude/skills/.trash, which added file system load that grew with each removal
  • Fixed the session name from /rename disappearing while Claude asks for permission or a plan decision, so side-by-side sessions stay identifiable
  • Fixed background sessions that fail to start being reported as a deleted daemon binary when the binary is still on disk
  • Fixed the tip and idle reminder about push notifications appearing when the push settings in /config are hidden or your organization has turned off Remote Control
  • Fixed ~/.claude/skills/.trash and ~/.claude/plugins/.trash growing without limit: each now holds about 1024 entries, whatever cleanupPeriodDays says
  • Fixed the Bash edit diff listing a whole file as changed when a CRLF file under git's line-ending conversion was re-saved unchanged or had one line edited
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed an idle session moving to another runner instead of pausing when the runner's request to pause it lost its connection before Anthropic answered
  • Improved memory use in long headless and SDK turns that run many subagents: the parent session no longer keeps each subagent's tool results until the turn ends
  • Improved prompt history: Ctrl+R now matches text inside collapsed [Pasted text] pills
  • Improved the /design-sync upload prompt to show the folder, the project and the files it will upload or delete
  • Improved /permissions review tab, now called Recently blocked: the footer says what Esc will do with marked rows
  • Improved auto mode's blocked calls: messages name the command, say Claude may retry and auto mode checks again, and point to /permissions to review
  • Improved permission prompts: a long reason takes fewer rows, so it pushes the command being approved off the screen on fewer terminals
  • Improved the cloud session error shown while a request refused for your claude.ai login is still being retried: it now also suggests claude auth login
  • Improved the behavior of stored claude.ai, Team, and Enterprise logins when MDM and remote settings differ on base URL or apiKeyHelper
  • Improved /config in agent view to say how to stop agent view opening by default
  • Improved session auto-titles: a session that starts with a skill or a prompt-based command such as /security-review now gets a title from it instead of staying untitled
  • Improved --resume speed and memory use on damaged transcripts
  • Improved /context speed in sessions with ten thousand or more MCP tools
  • Self-hosted runner: Improved the error shown when a session's branch isn't on the git remote: it now covers a never-pushed branch, says how to fix each case, and no longer suggests retrying
  • Updated the /claude-api skill: its Datadog setup for API tracing now sends the dd-llmobs-enabled: true header, as the Console does, and its ant install instructions drop the outdated macOS xattr step
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to advise printing y-axis tick labels in full under 10,000, and horizontal ones in full under a million where they fit
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to answer donut and pie chart requests with ranked bars or a segmented bar that prints its values
  • Changed Claude's file tools to ask before editing the local copy of your organization's server-managed settings, as they do for your settings files
  • Changed /ultrareview to check workspace trust before it runs git, as claude ultrareview does
  • Changed the Bash tool's shell to clear any inherited which alias or function and to stop passing exported which/unsetenv functions to commands, so which is the system command or zsh builtin
  • Changed /permissions Recently blocked to refuse approving a call you can't read in full, including one the terminal is too short to show
  • Changed auto mode in Cowork cloud sessions: a hook's allow of an MCP tool call now counts as no answer, so the classifier or a permission prompt decides
  • Changed hook if conditions such as Monitor(tail *) to match the Monitor tool's shell commands as Bash(tail *) matches Bash's
  • Changed the claude-api skill to ask to read a Managed Agents workflow run's workflow before changing the agent to improve that run
  • Changed flagged requests to retry on another model, not end in a refusal, when ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL, availableModels or deniedModels leaves only an older Opus model, or none
  • Changed idle compaction to also run for subscribers with telemetry turned off, and on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and LLM gateways once the one-hour prompt cache is on
  • Changed FORCE_HYPERLINK=false (also no and off) to turn hyperlinks off instead of on
  • macOS: Changed git grep in most commands that Claude runs to use the C locale, to avoid a reported memory leak in macOS's regex library on files that aren't valid UTF-8
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Clear authentication" for MCP servers reporting success when the saved sign-in could not be removed
  • [VSCode] Fixed missing spinner and Stop button while a queued message's hooks run
  • [VSCode] Fixed session group changes that cannot be saved, such as a delete, failing silently; an error notification now appears
  • [VSCode] Fixed Cmd+F / Ctrl+F not opening the find widget in the plan preview tab
  • [VSCode] Fixed the voice dictation shortcut (Ctrl+D) doing nothing under non-Latin keyboard layouts such as Russian, Greek or Hebrew
  • [VSCode] Fixed missed one-time saved scheduled tasks being deleted without asking when the extension opened without a chat
  • [VSCode] Changed CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_CFC_PROMPT to also stop the extension adding the Claude in Chrome instructions to a session's messages; the browser tools stay available
  • [Cloud sessions] Added an Include completed button to the Scheduled tasks page when finished one-off tasks are the only ones hidden, so you can show them without opening the Sort menu
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed recently used self-hosted environments never appearing among the recent environments on the new session card
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed cloud sessions reporting uncommitted changes every turn after Claude moved a branch to a commit it had pushed from another worktree
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the self-hosted environment details dialog in admin settings squeezing its content out of view in very short windows or at high zoom; the dialog now scrolls
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the permission mode picker staying on Auto after a running cloud or Remote Control session refused the switch; it now shows the mode in use and tells you
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved scheduled tasks: runs in Anthropic's cloud now load the plugins enabled on your claude.ai account
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved Test connection for GitHub Enterprise in admin settings to also connect the way cloud sessions do, and to warn you when that second test fails
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved cloud session transcripts: a rename row now names the new title, and repository and environment lists show as a table instead of one line of JSON
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed cloud sessions from the web, desktop and mobile apps to start even when a setup script exits with an error, instead of failing to start
  • [Remote Control] Fixed the permission mode button in Remote Control sessions showing the wrong mode until you typed; while your computer is online it now shows the real mode on open
  • [Claude Tag] Added a dismissible link to the Claude Tag API docs on the Bundles and Channels tabs in admin settings, for Enterprise organizations with Slack connected
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed @Claude !restart giving up after one failed workspace check in channels shared across Enterprise Grid workspaces; it now retries, then asks you to run it again
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed a second confirmation DM and channel note when you connect your Claude account from Slack twice from the same link within a few minutes
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed follow-up messages in Slack showing no sign of progress while Claude's session waits for a self-hosted runner; Claude now posts a wait notice in the thread
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude sometimes not answering a tag in its own thread in Slack Connect channels where both organizations have installed Claude
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Retry on plugin and skill pages in Claude Tag admin settings discarding unsaved access changes after a failed load; your edits now stay in place
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the repositories control in Claude Tag admin settings showing the same action twice; its menu now lists only what the button doesn't already do
release_highlights: Added permissions.blockWritesOutsideWorkingDirectories : Write, Edit and NotebookEdit refuse paths outside the working directories in every permission mode
Added an optional groups list to Claude apps gateway upstreams: only developers in the listed IdP groups are sent to that upstream, on failover too
Added guardrail_trace to Claude apps gateway Bedrock upstreams, to log which Amazon Bedrock guardrail filter fired on a request, without the matched text
